claim: The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway functions to degrade both abnormal and wild-type mRNAs.
source: The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway functions to degrade both abnormal and wild-type mRNAs.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of NMD function, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: NMD is essential for viability in most organisms.
source: NMD is essential for viability in most organisms, but the molecular basis for this requirement is unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the Introduction section.

claim: A single, conserved NMD target, the mRNA coding for GADD45, can account for lethality in Drosophila lacking core NMD genes.
source: Here we show that a single, conserved NMD target, the mRNA coding for the stress response factor growth arrest and DNA-damage inducible 45 (GADD45) can account for lethality in Drosophila lacking core NMD genes.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by genetic experiments showing suppression of lethality.

claim: Depletion of Gadd45 in mammalian cells rescues the cell survival defects associated with NMD knockdown.
source: Moreover, depletion of Gadd45 in mammalian cells rescues the cell survival defects associated with NMD knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by cell culture experiments with siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 3.

claim: Degradation of Gadd45 mRNA is the essential NMD function.
source: Our findings demonstrate that degradation of Gadd45 mRNA is the essential NMD function and, surprisingly, that the surveillance of abnormal mRNAs by this pathway is not necessarily required for viability.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the genetic suppression experiments and the fact that NMD function is not restored.

claim: The surveillance of abnormal mRNAs by NMD is not necessarily required for viability.
source: Our findings demonstrate that degradation of Gadd45 mRNA is the essential NMD function and, surprisingly, that the surveillance of abnormal mRNAs by this pathway is not necessarily required for viability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that viability can be restored without restoring NMD function.

claim: NMD is best known for its role as a quality control system, degrading abnormal mRNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs).
source: The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway is a trans-acting mechanism that destabilizes mRNAs, and is best known for its well-described role as a quality control system, degrading abnormal mRNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs) (Celik et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: NMD degrades many wild-type endogenous mRNAs and is an important aspect of their post-transcriptional regulation.
source: NMD also degrades many wild-type endogenous mRNAs and thus is an important aspect of their post-transcriptional (Peccarelli and Kebaara, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of either of the core NMD genes Upf1 (Rent1) or Upf2 causes lethality in most eukaryotes.
source: Loss of either of the core NMD genes Upf1 (Rent1) or Upf2 causes lethality in most eukaryotes (Kerényi et al., 2008; Medghalchi et al., 2001; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006; Weischenfeldt et al., 2008; Wittkopp et al., 2009), indicating regulation of mRNA stability by NMD is critical for viability.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Regulation of mRNA stability by NMD is critical for viability.
source: Loss of either of the core NMD genes Upf1 (Rent1) or Upf2 causes lethality in most eukaryotes (Kerényi et al., 2008; Medghalchi et al., 2001; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006; Weischenfeldt et al., 2008; Wittkopp et al., 2009), indicating regulation of mRNA stability by NMD is critical for viability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of NMD genes causes lethality.

claim: The relative contributions to lethality from ectopic stabilization of PTC-containing mRNAs or endogenous NMD targets in NMD mutants remains unclear.
source: However, the relative contributions to lethality from ectopic stabilization of PTC-containing mRNAs or endogenous NMD targets in NMD mutants remains unclear (Hwang and Maquat, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work discussing this open question.

claim: An unbiased genetic suppressor screen was performed to identify which ectopically stabilized mRNAs are responsible for inducing lethality in NMD mutants.
source: To identify which ectopically stabilized mRNAs are responsible for inducing lethality in NMD mutants, we performed an unbiased genetic suppressor screen seeking to restore viability in a Drosophila NMD mutant.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The Upf225G allele is a partially viable, hypomorphic allele of which 10% survive to adulthood.
source: To detect subtle increases in survival, we screened to suppress the lethality of animals mutant for the partially viable, hypomorphic Upf225G allele, of which 10% survive to adulthood (Chapin et al., 2014; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work characterizing this allele.

claim: Of the 376 deficiencies tested, covering more than half the genome, ~10% suppressed NMD mutant lethality.
source: Of the 376 deficiencies tested, covering more than half the genome, ~10% suppressed NMD mutant lethality (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The suppression effect could not be explained by a reduction in overall mRNA load.
source: The suppression effect could not be explained by a reduction in overall mRNA load, as there was only a weak correlation between the increase in mRNAs expressed from a genomic region upon loss of NMD function and the strength of suppression when that region was removed by a deficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Deficiencies that suppressed NMD-mutant lethality clustered in three genomic regions.
source: Rather, deficiencies that suppressed NMD-mutant lethality clustered in three genomic regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NMD mutant lethality is not the result of a global excess of nonspecific mRNAs, but rather is mediated by specific genes residing within the few identified regions.
source: These findings suggest that NMD mutant lethality is not the result of a global excess of nonspecific mRNAs, but rather is mediated by specific genes residing within the few identified regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering of suppressing deficiencies and lack of correlation with overall mRNA load.

claim: Gadd45 is the only gene located within the suppressing regions that has increased expression levels in an NMD mutant and is a direct NMD target.
source: We expected that any specific genes mediating NMD-mutant lethality would have increased expression levels in an NMD mutant and be a direct NMD target. The only gene located within the suppressing regions to fit these criteria is Gadd45 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C) (Chapin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by expression data and NMD targeting assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Gadd45F17 is a null allele that completely removes the Gadd45 coding region.
source: To determine if NMD targeting of Gadd45 mRNA is critical for viability, we generated a Gadd45 null allele, F17, which completely removes the Gadd45 coding region (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and eliminates Gadd45 mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by molecular characterization and expression data shown in the figures.

claim: Gadd45F17 eliminates Gadd45 mRNA expression.
source: To determine if NMD targeting of Gadd45 mRNA is critical for viability, we generated a Gadd45 null allele, F17, which completely removes the Gadd45 coding region (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and eliminates Gadd45 mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: As a heterozygote, Gadd45F17 suppressed Upf225G lethality as strongly as the corresponding deficiency identified by the screen.
source: As a heterozygote, Gadd45F17 suppressed Upf225Glethality as strongly as the corresponding deficiency identified by our screen (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gadd45F17 homozygous mutants are fully viable.
source: We found that Gadd45F17 homozygous mutants are fully viable (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), allowing us to test complete loss of Gadd45 for the suppression of NMD-mutant lethality.
evidence: This is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Homozygous Gadd45F17 restored full viability to Upf225G mutants.
source: Homozygous Gadd45F17 restored full viability to Upf225Gmutants, and remarkably even partially suppressed the complete lethality observed in null Upf1 and Upf2 mutants (Frizzell et al., 2012; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Homozygous Gadd45F17 partially suppressed the complete lethality observed in null Upf1 and Upf2 mutants.
source: Homozygous Gadd45F17 restored full viability to Upf225Gmutants, and remarkably even partially suppressed the complete lethality observed in null Upf1 and Upf2 mutants (Frizzell et al., 2012; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neither reducing nor eliminating Gadd45 restored NMD function to Upf225G mutants.
source: Importantly, neither reducing nor eliminating Gadd45 restored NMD function to Upf225G mutants, as measured by the expression of both an endogenous NMD target (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) and PTC-containing mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claim: In mammals, GADD45 activates the MTK1/MEKK4 kinase in a well-defined stress response pathway.
source: In mammals, GADD45 activates the MTK1/MEKK4 kinase in a well-defined stress response pathway (Takekawa and Saito, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The Drosophila MTK1 orthologue, Mekk1, resides within another Upf225G suppressing region.
source: Strikingly, the Drosophila MTK1 orthologue, Mekk1, resides within another Upf225G suppressing region (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the mapping data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mekk1 null mutants suppressed Upf1 and Upf2 mutant lethality.
source: Similar to Gadd45, we found that Mekk1 null mutants (Inoue et al., 2001) suppressed Upf1 and Upf2 mutant lethality (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by viability data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Suppression by Mekk1 null mutants was not as strong as that caused by a loss of Gadd45.
source: This suppression was not as strong as that caused by a loss of Gadd45, revealing that although MEKK1 mediates NMD mutant lethality, it is likely that GADD45 has additional downstream effectors that influence viability.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the suppression strength shown in Figure 1D and 1F.

claim: GADD45 likely has additional downstream effectors beyond MEKK1 that influence viability.
source: This suppression was not as strong as that caused by a loss of Gadd45, revealing that although MEKK1 mediates NMD mutant lethality, it is likely that GADD45 has additional downstream effectors that influence viability.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential suppression strength.

claim: Increased Gadd45 mRNA stability is the major factor inducing NMD mutant lethality, primarily via increased MEKK1 activity.
source: Overall, our findings reveal that increased Gadd45 mRNA stability is the major factor inducing NMD mutant lethality, primarily via increased MEKK1 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic suppression experiments with both Gadd45 and Mekk1.

claim: Activation of MTK1 in mammals triggers a MAPK signaling cascade that promotes apoptosis.
source: Activation of MTK1 in mammals triggers a MAPK signaling cascade that promotes apoptosis (Takekawa and Saito, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Over-expression of Gadd45 in Drosophila induces apoptosis.
source: Over-expression of Gadd45 in Drosophila also induces apoptosis (Peretz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Drosophila cells lacking NMD function show excess cell death in a variety of tissues.
source: Interestingly, Drosophila cells lacking NMD function show excess cell death in a variety of tissues (Avery et al., 2011; Frizzell et al., 2012; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Wing imaginal discs from Upf225G mutant third instar larvae show elevated levels of cell death compared to controls.
source: To test if increased Gadd45 contributes to this excess death, we used TUNEL staining to examine cell death in wing imaginal discs from Upf225G mutant third instar larvae. This analysis revealed elevated levels of cell death compared to controls (Figure 2A, B, E), and this defect was completely suppressed by Gadd45F17 (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2A, B, E.

claim: The elevated cell death in Upf225G mutant wing discs was completely suppressed by Gadd45F17.
source: To test if increased Gadd45 contributes to this excess death, we used TUNEL staining to examine cell death in wing imaginal discs from Upf225G mutant third instar larvae. This analysis revealed elevated levels of cell death compared to controls (Figure 2A, B, E), and this defect was completely suppressed by Gadd45F17 (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: Smg5 mutant wing discs showed elevated TUNEL signal, which was eliminated by loss of Gadd45.
source: To confirm that, this effect was not specific to the Upf2 gene or 25G allele, we examined the wing discs in mutants of another essential NMD gene, Smg5. We found that Smg5 discs also showed elevated TUNEL signal, which was eliminated by loss of Gadd45 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Excess Gadd45 accounts for ectopic cell death in NMD mutant tissues.
source: These results demonstrate that excess Gadd45 accounts for ectopic cell death in NMD mutant tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of cell death by Gadd45 loss in multiple NMD mutant backgrounds.

claim: NMD is required for proper development of eye cells, as clonal patches of NMD mutant cells in eyes are reduced in size.
source: To test if Gadd45-induced cell death is the only cellular defect in NMD mutants, we examined NMD function in the developing eye. NMD is required for proper development of eye cells, as clonal patches of NMD mutant cells in eyes are reduced in size (Frizzell et al., 2012; Metzstein and Krasnow, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gadd45 is partially responsible for the reduced size of eye-cell clones lacking NMD activity.
source: We found that Gadd45 is partially responsible for this defect, as the size of eye-cell clones lacking NMD activity in a Gadd45F17 background was increased, although not fully restored (Figure 2F–J).
evidence: This is supported by eye clone size data shown in Figure 2F–J.

claim: Some, but not all, defects associated with loss of NMD are dependent on Gadd45.
source: These results indicate that some, but not all, defects associated with loss of NMD are dependent on Gadd45.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial suppression of eye clone size defects.

claim: Gadd45 is one of the few genes that is directly regulated by NMD in both flies and mammals.
source: Gadd45 is one of the few genes that is directly regulated by NMD in both flies and mammals (Huang et al., 2011; Tani et al., 2012; Viegas et al., 2007), raising the possibility that excess Gadd45 abundance may also contribute to the NMD-mutant lethality observed in mammalian cells (Azzalin and Lingner, 2006; Li et al., 2015; Medghalchi et al., 2001; Weischenfeldt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gadd45b mRNA is expressed at least 10-fold higher than any other Gadd45 paralogue in NIH-3T3 cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we analyzed the effects of Gadd45 and Upf1 depletion in mouse NIH-3T3 cells. Gadd45b mRNA (also known as MyD118), which is expressed at least 10-fold higher than any other Gadd45 paralogue in these cells (Yue et al., 2014), was degraded rapidly in a partially Upf1-dependent manner after transcription was blocked with actinomycin D (Figure 3A), and had increased expression during Upf1 knockdown (Figure 3D), confirming it is sensitive to NMD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Gadd45b mRNA was degraded rapidly in a partially Upf1-dependent manner after transcription was blocked with actinomycin D.
source: Gadd45b mRNA (also known as MyD118), which is expressed at least 10-fold higher than any other Gadd45 paralogue in these cells (Yue et al., 2014), was degraded rapidly in a partially Upf1-dependent manner after transcription was blocked with actinomycin D (Figure 3A), and had increased expression during Upf1 knockdown (Figure 3D), confirming it is sensitive to NMD.
evidence: This is supported by actinomycin D decay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gadd45b had increased expression during Upf1 knockdown, confirming it is sensitive to NMD.
source: Gadd45b mRNA (also known as MyD118), which is expressed at least 10-fold higher than any other Gadd45 paralogue in these cells (Yue et al., 2014), was degraded rapidly in a partially Upf1-dependent manner after transcription was blocked with actinomycin D (Figure 3A), and had increased expression during Upf1 knockdown (Figure 3D), confirming it is sensitive to NMD.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Transfection of 3T3 cells with siRNAs targeting Upf1 resulted in significant reduction in cell counts after 48 hr.
source: We found that transfection of 3T3 cells with siRNAs targeting Upf1 resulted in significant reduction in cell counts after 48 hr (Figure 3B), but co-transfection with siRNAs targeting both Upf1 and Gadd45b largely reversed this effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Co-transfection with siRNAs targeting both Upf1 and Gadd45b largely reversed the reduction in cell counts caused by Upf1 knockdown.
source: We found that transfection of 3T3 cells with siRNAs targeting Upf1 resulted in significant reduction in cell counts after 48 hr (Figure 3B), but co-transfection with siRNAs targeting both Upf1 and Gadd45b largely reversed this effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduction in cell counts in Upf1 knockdown was primarily due to increased cell death.
source: The reduction in cell counts was primarily due to increased cell death, as we found that ~25% of cells transfected with Upf1 siRNA were undergoing apoptosis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ~25% of cells transfected with Upf1 siRNA were undergoing apoptosis.
source: The reduction in cell counts was primarily due to increased cell death, as we found that ~25% of cells transfected with Upf1 siRNA were undergoing apoptosis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Co-transfection of siRNA targeting Gadd45b almost entirely eliminated the increase in apoptosis in Upf1-knockdown cells.
source: Co-transfection of siRNA targeting Gadd45b almost entirely eliminated this increase (Figure 3C), indicating the excess apoptosis observed in Upf1-knockdown cells was mostly due to increased Gadd45 activity.
evidence: This is supported by annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The excess apoptosis observed in Upf1-knockdown cells was mostly due to increased Gadd45 activity.
source: Co-transfection of siRNA targeting Gadd45b almost entirely eliminated this increase (Figure 3C), indicating the excess apoptosis observed in Upf1-knockdown cells was mostly due to increased Gadd45 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of apoptosis by Gadd45b knockdown.

claim: Loss of NMD may lead to both Gadd45b-dependent cell death as well as a Gadd45b-independent effect on proliferation.
source: However, while Gadd45b knockdown very greatly suppresses this excess death, it does not as fully rescue cell numbers, suggesting loss of NMD may lead to both Gadd45b-dependent cell death as well as a Gadd45b-independent effect on proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue of cell death versus cell numbers.

claim: Upf1 mRNA expression was equivalently reduced in both the single and double knockdown experiments in 3T3 cells.
source: Importantly, Upf1 mRNA expression was equivalently reduced and the expression of the mammalian endogenous NMD targets Rassf1 and CRCP (Tani et al., 2012) was equivalently increased in both the single and double knockdown experiments (Figure 3D), indicating that the restoration of viability was not due to a recovery of NMD pathway activity.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The expression of the mammalian endogenous NMD targets Rassf1 and CRCP was equivalently increased in both the single and double knockdown experiments in 3T3 cells.
source: Importantly, Upf1 mRNA expression was equivalently reduced and the expression of the mammalian endogenous NMD targets Rassf1 and CRCP (Tani et al., 2012) was equivalently increased in both the single and double knockdown experiments (Figure 3D), indicating that the restoration of viability was not due to a recovery of NMD pathway activity.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The restoration of viability in 3T3 cells was not due to a recovery of NMD pathway activity.
source: Importantly, Upf1 mRNA expression was equivalently reduced and the expression of the mammalian endogenous NMD targets Rassf1 and CRCP (Tani et al., 2012) was equivalently increased in both the single and double knockdown experiments (Figure 3D), indicating that the restoration of viability was not due to a recovery of NMD pathway activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the equivalent NMD target expression in single and double knockdowns.

claim: siRNA knockdown of UPF1 in HEK293 cells led to increased GADD45A expression and reduced cell numbers compared to control siRNA.
source: To extend our analysis to other mammalian cells, we analyzed the role of Gadd45 mediating the effects of loss of NMD in HEK293 cells. We found, similarly to 3T3 cells, that siRNA knockdown of UPF1 in HEK293 cells led to increased GADD45A expression and reduced cell numbers compared to control siRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Co-transfection with UPF1 siRNA and GADD45A siRNA did not further reduce cell count in HEK293 cells compared to GADD45A siRNA alone.
source: Although transfection of siRNA targeting GADD45A alone slightly reduced HEK293 cell numbers, co-transfection with UPF1 siRNA did not further reduce cell count (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and UPF1 expression was equivalently reduced in the single and double knockdown conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: UPF1 expression was equivalently reduced in the single and double knockdown conditions in HEK293 cells.
source: Although transfection of siRNA targeting GADD45A alone slightly reduced HEK293 cell numbers, co-transfection with UPF1 siRNA did not further reduce cell count (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and UPF1 expression was equivalently reduced in the single and double knockdown conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: UPF1 knockdown is no longer detrimental to HEK293 cell viability in the absence of GADD45A expression.
source: These results suggest that UPF1 knockdown is no longer detrimental to HEK293 cell viability in the absence of GADD45A expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additional cell count reduction in the double knockdown.

claim: Increased expression of mammalian Gadd45 genes contributes to lethality in NMD-deficient mouse and human cells.
source: We conclude that increased expression of mammalian Gadd45 genes contributes to lethality in NMD-deficient mouse and human cells, as Gadd45 does in Drosophila.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments in both 3T3 and HEK293 cells.

claim: Viability can be restored to Drosophila lacking core NMD factors when a single endogenous NMD target, Gadd45, is eliminated.
source: Deconvoluting the contributions to organismal viability of the PTC-surveillance versus gene-regulatory functions of NMD has been historically difficult (Hwang and Maquat, 2011). Here, we show that viability can be restored to Drosophila lacking core NMD factors when a single endogenous NMD target, Gadd45, is eliminated, and that the requirement for the regulation of Gadd45 by NMD is evolutionarily conserved from flies to mammals.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the genetic experiments.

claim: The requirement for the regulation of Gadd45 by NMD is evolutionarily conserved from flies to mammals.
source: Here, we show that viability can be restored to Drosophila lacking core NMD factors when a single endogenous NMD target, Gadd45, is eliminated, and that the requirement for the regulation of Gadd45 by NMD is evolutionarily conserved from flies to mammals.
evidence: This is supported by the experiments in both Drosophila and mammalian cells.

claim: Up-regulation of Gadd45 is a major factor contributing to lethality when NMD activity is lost.
source: Although our data suggest that up-regulation of Gadd45 is a major factor contributing to lethality when NMD activity is lost, it is likely that other NMD targets also contribute to the observed lethality.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic suppression data.

claim: Other NMD targets likely also contribute to the observed lethality when NMD activity is lost.
source: Although our data suggest that up-regulation of Gadd45 is a major factor contributing to lethality when NMD activity is lost, it is likely that other NMD targets also contribute to the observed lethality.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete suppression in null mutants.

claim: Viability is not restored to 100% in null Upf1; or Upf2; Gadd45 double mutants.
source: In particular, viability is not restored to 100% in null Upf1; or Upf2; Gadd45 double mutants.
evidence: This is supported by the viability data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of Gadd45 suppresses programmed cell death caused by defects in NMD, but not additional cell cycle defects.
source: In addition, loss of Gadd45 suppresses programmed cell death caused by defects in NMD, but not additional cell cycle defects, as implied by the incomplete suppression in the Drosophila eye and mammalian cell culture.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial suppression of eye clone size and cell proliferation defects.

claim: Defects in the cell cycle may be particularly pronounced during the development of certain tissue, or specific developmental stages.
source: Such defects in the cell cycle may be particularly pronounced during the development of certain tissue, or specific developmental stages.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed tissue-specific effects.

claim: NMD has been reported to have differing stage and tissue-specific activities.
source: Indeed, NMD has been reported to have differing stage and tissue- specific activities (Bao et al., 2015; Bruno et al., 2011; Colak et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The benefit for a mechanism regulating Gadd45 expression may lie in a function of NMD in restricting viral growth.
source: The benefit for such a mechanism regulating Gadd45 expression may lie in a function of NMD in restricting viral growth (Balistreri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior work on NMD and viral restriction.

claim: Viruses encode trans-acting factors to inhibit NMD.
source: Because viruses encode trans-acting factors to inhibit NMD (Mocquet et al., 2012), the resulting accumulation of GADD45 in infected cells may act as a "molecular tripwire" that rapidly elicits a stress response and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The accumulation of GADD45 in infected cells may act as a "molecular tripwire" that rapidly elicits a stress response and cell death.
source: Because viruses encode trans-acting factors to inhibit NMD (Mocquet et al., 2012), the resulting accumulation of GADD45 in infected cells may act as a "molecular tripwire" that rapidly elicits a stress response and cell death.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known functions of GADD45 and NMD.

claim: Regulating responses to infection may underlie a conserved essential function of NMD.
source: This outcome suggests that regulating responses to infection may underlie a conserved essential function of NMD.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed molecular tripwire mechanism.

claim: Restriction of pathogens via NMD extends to plants.
source: Intriguingly, restriction of pathogens via NMD extends to plants (Garcia et al., 2014), where NMD mutant lethality in A. thaliana, which do not encode Gadd45 orthologues, may be caused by the overexpression of a subset of immune-related intracellular nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors, some of which are endogenous NMD targets (Gloggnitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NMD mutant lethality in A. thaliana may be caused by the overexpression of a subset of immune-related intracellular nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors, some of which are endogenous NMD targets.
source: Intriguingly, restriction of pathogens via NMD extends to plants (Garcia et al., 2014), where NMD mutant lethality in A. thaliana, which do not encode Gadd45 orthologues, may be caused by the overexpression of a subset of immune-related intracellular nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors, some of which are endogenous NMD targets (Gloggnitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A. thaliana do not encode Gadd45 orthologues.
source: Intriguingly, restriction of pathogens via NMD extends to plants (Garcia et al., 2014), where NMD mutant lethality in A. thaliana, which do not encode Gadd45 orthologues, may be caused by the overexpression of a subset of immune-related intracellular nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors, some of which are endogenous NMD targets (Gloggnitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on genomic knowledge.

claim: Eukaryotes that do not rely on the activation of programmed cell death to protect against viruses, such as S. cerevisiae, S. pombe, and C. elegans, do not require NMD for viability.
source: In contrast, eukaryotes that do not rely on the activation of programmed cell death to protect against viruses, such as S. cerevisiae, S. pombe, and C. elegans, do not require NMD for viability (Hodgkin et al., 1989; Leeds et al., 1991; Mendell et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NMD and Gadd45 may have a novel role in immune responses, triggering the death of infected cells during pathogenic challenges.
source: Together these observations suggest a potential novel role for NMD and Gadd45 in immune responses, triggering the death of infected cells during pathogenic challenges.
evidence: This is speculation based on the various observations about NMD, Gadd45, and pathogen restriction.

claim: Restoring the expression of PTC-containing alleles via NMD inhibition has been proposed as a promising therapy for a wide range of recessive genetic diseases.
source: Restoring the expression of PTC-containing alleles via NMD inhibition has been proposed as a promising therapy for a wide range of recessive genetic diseases (Keeling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Translation of stable PTC-containing mRNAs would produce truncated proteins that may be partially functional and alleviate disease symptoms normally caused by complete loss of the protein.
source: Translation of stable PTC-containing mRNAs would produce truncated proteins that may be partially functional and alleviate disease symptoms normally caused by complete loss of the protein.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential therapeutic mechanism.

claim: The essential function for NMD in viability has raised the concern that NMD inhibition therapies may have prohibitive side effects.
source: However, the essential function for NMD in viability has raised the concern that these therapies may have prohibitive side effects.
evidence: This is inference based on the known essential function of NMD.

claim: Inhibiting both the NMD and Gadd45 pathways in combination could provide an effective and safe treatment for patients with debilitating genetic disorders.
source: Our findings reveal a molecular basis for dealing with this obstacle by suggesting that inhibiting both the NMD and Gadd45 pathways (Tornatore et al., 2014) in combination could provide an effective and safe treatment for patients with debilitating genetic disorders.
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic implications based on the study's findings.

claim: Gadd45 mRNA expression is increased 16.7-fold in Upf225G mutants.
source: Gadd45 mRNA expression is increased 16.7-fold in Upf225G mutants, and is eliminated by Gadd45F17 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.
